'''BEAT''' is a music-oriented [[esoteric programming language]] whose complete
interpreter runs from a 1.44 MB floppy disk image in 16-bit real mode. It does
not run on top of an operating system: the boot sector loads the BEAT engine,
and the engine drives the machine's internal speaker through the 8253 timer and
port <code>61h</code>.

== Program format ==

A BEAT program is a byte string stored in sector 4 of the disk image. The
program is limited to 511 bytes followed by a NUL terminator. The engine starts
at <code>0x0600</code>; the program is independent from the engine sectors, so
the music can be changed without rebuilding the interpreter.

The reference source contains nine catalogue programs. The first program is a
scale:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
T4D9N440.N494.N523.N587.N659.N698.N784.H
</syntaxhighlight>

== Disk layout ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Sector !! Address !! Content
|-
| 1 || <code>0x000</code> || FAT12-compatible boot sector and loader
|-
| 2-3 || <code>0x200</code> || BEAT engine, loaded at <code>0x0100</code>
|-
| 4 || <code>0x400</code> || User program, up to 511 bytes plus NUL
|}

At runtime the engine uses the following memory areas:

{| class="wikitable"
! Address !! Purpose
|-
| <code>0x0000-0x04FF</code> || IVT and BIOS Data Area; untouched by the engine
|-
| <code>0x0100</code> || Loaded BEAT engine
|-
| <code>0x0500</code> || Instruction pointer, register, tempo, duration and tape pointer
|-
| <code>0x0600</code> || Program loaded from sector 4
|-
| <code>0x0800</code> || 2 KB runtime tape
|}

== Execution model ==

The machine has one 16-bit register and a 2 KB tape. Arithmetic instructions
operate on the register. <code>R</code> and <code>W</code> connect the register to
the tape, allowing a value to be stored and later reused as a note frequency or
loop state.

The speaker is driven by the 8253 programmable interval timer. Requested
frequencies are converted to integer timer divisors, so the physical output is
the frequency the hardware can express rather than necessarily the requested
frequency. Durations use BIOS ticks at approximately 18.2065 Hz.

== Instructions ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Instruction !! Effect
|-
| <code>&gt;</code>, <code>&lt;</code> || Move the tape pointer
|-
| <code>+</code>, <code>-</code> || Increment or decrement the register
|-
| <code>.</code> || Play the register as a frequency
|-
| <code>,</code> || Keyboard input; the reference no-console path reads zero
|-
| <code>[</code>, <code>]</code> || Loop while the register is non-zero
|-
| <code>T&lt;n&gt;</code> || Select tempo table entry 0-9
|-
| <code>D&lt;n&gt;</code> || Set note duration 0-9
|-
| <code>N&lt;hz&gt;</code> || Load a decimal frequency, for example <code>N440</code>
|-
| <code>P</code> || Pause for the current duration
|-
| <code>R</code> || Read the tape cell into the register
|-
| <code>W</code> || Write the low byte of the register to the tape
|-
| <code>J</code> || Unconditional absolute jump
|-
| <code>Z</code> || Jump if the register is zero
|-
| <code>S</code> || Toggle the speaker state and sustain the last timer tone
|-
| <code>H</code> || Stop the machine
|}

The Brainfuck-like loop instructions are register loops, not ordinary
multi-cell Brainfuck loops. The tape stores only the low byte of a register
value, from 0 through 255.

<code>J</code> and <code>Z</code> use absolute addresses based on the program's
fixed load address. Programs using them are therefore not generally relocatable
inside the sector.

== I/O and output ==

BEAT has no conventional text stdout. Its observable output is the sound
produced by the internal speaker. A run can be observed through:

* the physical or emulated speaker;
* the reference simulator's list of frequency-duration events;
* a rendered WAV file;
* QEMU audio capture and note analysis.

== Building and running ==

The image is built from <code>BEAT.asm</code> with NASM:

<syntaxhighlight lang="sh">
./build.sh
qemu-system-i386 -fda BEAT.img
</syntaxhighlight>

The reference simulator can run a program without booting QEMU:

<syntaxhighlight lang="sh">
python tools/beat_sim.py 'T4D9N440.N494.N523.H' scale.wav
</syntaxhighlight>

The simulator is a semantic reference, not the final hardware test. The
hardware-facing verification is:

<syntaxhighlight lang="sh">
python tools/test_qemu.py
</syntaxhighlight>

== Changing a program without rebuilding ==

The program occupies its own sector. A replacement program can be patched into
an existing image:

<syntaxhighlight lang="sh">
python tools/patch_sector4.py BEAT.img program.beat output.img
qemu-system-i386 -fda output.img
</syntaxhighlight>

The patcher preserves the boot signature and rejects programs larger than the
sector budget.

== FLOW integration ==

<code>tools/flow2beat.py</code> is an adapter from a FLOW execution trace to a
BEAT program. It maps particle positions to pitches, particle density to
tempo, state changes to tape operations, and particle deaths to pauses. This is
an output adapter, not a claim that BEAT and FLOW share the same execution
semantics.

<syntaxhighlight lang="sh">
python tools/flow2beat.py execution.trace.json -o flow.beat
python tools/patch_sector4.py BEAT.img flow.beat BEAT_FLOW.img
qemu-system-i386 -fda BEAT_FLOW.img
</syntaxhighlight>

The generated program is still subject to the 511-byte sector limit. Events
that do not fit are not encoded in the output program.

== Computational status ==

No computational-class claim is made here. BEAT has arithmetic, loops, mutable
tape storage and absolute jumps, but its execution is constrained by the disk
program size and the machine's runtime model.

== Implementation ==

The reference implementation is in [https://github.com/DannyBaanks/BEAT BEAT]
and is released under the MIT license. The simulator and analysis tools live in
<code>tools/</code>; they verify behavior but are not part of the disk image
build chain.
